region.zh: 阿卡迪亞庫勒涅山（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homeric Hymns XIX (To Pan), trans. Andrew Lang (1899)

summary.en: Tell me, Muse, concerning the dear son of Hermes, the goat-footed, the twy-horned, the lover of the din of revel, who haunts the wooded dells with dancing nymphs that tread the crests of the steep cliffs, calling upon Pan the pastoral god of the long wild hair. Lord is he of every snowy crest and mountain peak and rocky path; he ranges over the high white hills and chases the wild beasts with keen eye, and at evening returns piping from the chase. The mountain nymphs go wandering with him by the dark water of the well, while the echo moans along the mountain crest; on his back he wears the tawny hide of a lynx. They sing of the blessed gods and of high Olympus, and above all of boon Hermes: how he came to many-fountained Arcadia, the mother of sheep, where his Cyllenian demesne is, and there, god as he was, he shepherded the fleecy sheep, the thrall of a mortal man; for soft desire had come upon him to wed the fair-haired daughter of Dryops, and the glad nuptials he accomplished, and to Hermes in the hall she bore a dear son. From his birth he was a marvel to behold: goat-footed, twy-horned, a loud speaker, a sweet laugher. Then the nurse leaped up and fled when she saw his wild face and bearded chin. But him did boon Hermes straightway take in his hands and bear, and gladly did he rejoice at heart. Swiftly to the dwellings of the gods went he, bearing the babe hidden in the thick skins of mountain hares; there he sat down by Zeus and the other immortals, and showed his child, and all the immortals were glad at heart, and chiefly the Bacchic Dionysus. Pan they called the babe to name, because he had made glad the hearts of all of them.
summary.zh: 繆斯啊，請歌頌赫爾墨斯之愛子：羊足雙角、喜好狂歡之聲的潘神，與舞於崖頂之仙女們漫遊林谷；他為雪峰、山巔與巉岩之主，日逐野獸，暮攜蘆笛而歸；仙女們伴其於幽泉旁歌唱，回聲在山脊嗚咽；背披猞猁皮。歌中頌諸神與奧林波斯，尤頌赫爾墨斯：他至多泉的阿卡迪亞（羊之母）、其庫勒涅領地，化身凡人為人牧羊；因戀德律俄普斯之金髮女兒而結良緣，生下一子。此子生而奇異：羊足、雙角、聲宏、愛笑。乳母見其野面與鬍鬚驚逃；赫爾墨斯抱起嬰兒、以野兔厚皮裹之，攜至奧林波斯示於宙斯與眾神，眾神皆喜，尤以酒神狄俄尼索斯為甚；因其使眾心皆悅，遂名之曰潘（Pan）。

Lord is he of every snowy crest and mountain peak and rocky path.

passages.text: Hither and thither he goes through the thick copses, sometimes being drawn to the still waters, and sometimes faring through the lofty crags he climbs the highest peak whence the flocks are seen below; ever he ranges over the high white hills, and ever among the knolls he chases and slays the wild beasts, the god with keen eye, and at evening returns piping from the chase, breathing sweet strains on the reeds. In song that bird cannot excel him which, among the leaves of the blossoming springtide, pours forth her plaint and her honey-sweet song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homeric Hymns XIX, To Pan (Lang 1899); not verbatim.

passages.text: With him then the mountain nymphs, the shrill singers, go wandering with light feet, and sing at the side of the dark water of the well, while the echo moans along the mountain crest, and the god leaps hither and thither, and goes into the midst, with many a step of the dance. On his back he wears the tawny hide of a lynx, and his heart rejoices with shrill songs in the soft meadow where crocus and fragrant hyacinth bloom all mingled amidst the grass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homeric Hymns XIX, To Pan (Lang 1899); not verbatim.

passages.text: They sing of the blessed gods and of high Olympus, and above all do they sing of boon Hermes, how he is the fleet herald of all the gods, and how he came to many-fountained Arcadia, the mother of sheep, where is his Cyllenian demesne, and there he, god as he was, shepherded the fleecy sheep, the thrall of a mortal man; for soft desire had come upon him to wed the fair-haired daughter of Dryops, and the glad nuptials he accomplished, and to Hermes in the hall she bare a dear son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homeric Hymns XIX, To Pan (Lang 1899); not verbatim.

title.zh: 北風玻瑞阿斯與俄里堤亞

region.zh: 雅典至色雷斯（象徵性定位）

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)

summary.en: Boreas, not obtaining the consent of Erectheus, king of Athens, for the marriage of his daughter, takes the princess Orithyia in his arms and carries her away into Thrace, and by her has two sons, Calais and Zethes, who have wings like their father and afterwards embark with Jason in search of the Golden Fleece. Long was the god without his much-loved Orithyia, while he was entreating rather than using force. At last, in the native rage of his winds, he said: 'Why did I relinquish my own weapons, my violence, my strength, my anger, and my threatening spirit, and turn to prayers, the employment of which ill becomes me? Violence is suitable for me; by violence do I dispel the lowering clouds, arouse the seas, overthrow the knotted oaks, and harden the snow.' Boreas, having said these words, or some not less high-sounding than these, shakes his wings, by the motion of which all the earth is fanned and the wide sea becomes ruffled; and the lover, drawing his dusty mantle over the high tops of mountains, sweeps the ground, and, wrapt in darkness, embraces with his tawny wings Orithyia as she trembles with fear.
summary.zh: 北風玻瑞阿斯向雅典王厄瑞克透斯求娶其女俄里堤亞，未獲允准；女神為其所愛良久，他先以言求、不施暴。終於，他以風之暴怒自言：「為何棄我之暴力與怒氣而屈膝求婚？暴力方合我——我以暴力散雲、興海、倒橡樹、凝霜雪。」言罷振翼，大地震盪、海洋翻騰；以塵罩高山、以黑暗裹身，張黃褐之翼抱走戰慄的俄里堤亞，飛往色雷斯；她為其生下雙子卡萊斯與仄忒斯，皆有父之翼，後隨伊阿宋遠征取金羊毛。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Erectheus received the sceptre of that country, and the government of the state; it is a matter of doubt whether he was more powerful through his justice, or by his mighty arms. He had begotten four sons, and as many of the female sex: but the beauty of two of them was equal. Of these, Cephalus, the son of Aeolus, was blessed with Procris for his wife; and Tereus and the Thracians were an obstacle to Boreas; and long was that God without his much-loved Orithyia, while he was entreating, and choosing rather to use prayers than force.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable VII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: But when nothing was effected by blandishments, terrible with that rage which is his wont, and but too natural with that wind, he said: 'And this is deservedly done; for why did I relinquish my own weapons, my violence, my strength, my anger, and my threatening spirit, and turn to prayers, the employment of which ill becomes me? Violence is suitable for me; by violence do I dispel the lowering clouds, by violence do I arouse the seas, and overthrow the knotted oaks, and harden the snow, and beat the earth with hail. I too, when I have met with my brothers in the open air, struggle with efforts so great that the intermediate sky thunders again with our onset, and fires flash, struck forth from the hollow clouds. I too, when I have descended into the hollow recesses of the earth, and in my rage have placed my back against its lowest depths, disturb the shades below, and the whole globe with earthquakes. By these means should I have sought this alliance; and Erectheus ought not to have been entreated to be my father-in-law, but made so by force.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable VII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Boreas, having said these words, or some not less high-sounding than these, shakes his wings, by the motion of which all the earth is fanned, and the wide sea becomes ruffled; and the lover, drawing his dusty mantle over the high tops of mountains, sweeps the ground, and, wrapt in darkness, embraces with his tawny wings Orithyia as she trembles with fear. As she flies, his flame, being agitated, burns more fiercely. Nor does the ravisher check the reins of his airy course, before he reaches the people and the walls of the Ciconians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable VII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: There, too, is the Actaean damsel made the wife of the cold sovereign, and afterwards a mother, bringing forth twins at a birth, who have the wings of their father, the rest like their mother. Yet they say that these wings were not produced together with their bodies; and while their long beard, with its yellow hair, was away, the boys Calais and Zethes were without feathers. But soon after, at once, wings began to enclose both their sides, after the manner of birds; and at once their cheeks began to grow yellow with down. When, therefore, the boyish season of youth was passed, they sought, with the Minyae, along the sea before unmoved, in the first ship that existed, the fleece that glittered with shining hair of gold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable VII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Triptolemus and the King of Scythia
title.zh: 特里普托勒摩斯與斯基泰王

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)

summary.en: The fertile Goddess yoked two dragons to her chariot, curbed their mouths with bridles, and was borne through the mid-air of heaven and earth, guiding her light chariot to the Tritonian citadel, to Triptolemus; and she ordered him to scatter the seeds entrusted to him, partly in the fallow ground, partly in the ground restored to cultivation after so long a time. Now the youth had been borne on high over Europe and the lands of Asia, and he arrived at the coast of Scythia: Lyncus was the king there. Asked whence he came and his name and country, he said: 'My country is the famous Athens, my name is Triptolemus. I came neither in a ship through the waves nor on foot by land; the pervious sky made a way for me. I bring the gifts of Ceres, which, scattered over the wide fields, are to yield you fruitful harvests and wholesome food.' The barbarian envied him, and, that he himself might be deemed the author of so great a benefit, received him with hospitality; and when, overpowered with sleep, he attacked him with the sword, Ceres changed him into a lynx, and sent the Mopsopian youth on his way again.
summary.zh: 女神刻瑞斯以雙龍駕車，經天地半空至雅典衛城見特里普托勒摩斯，命其將種子播於休耕之地與久荒之土。少年飛越歐洲與亞洲，至斯基泰海岸；該地王為林科斯。特里普托勒摩斯自報家門，言其以天路而行、攜刻瑞斯贈禮使田野豐產。蠻王心生嫉妒，欲獨享功勞，故熱情款待、待其沉睡而持劍刺之；女神遂將林科斯化為猞猁猻，再遣少年騰空而去。

Being asked whence he came, and the occasion of his coming, and his name, and his country, he said: 'My country is the famous Athens, my name is Triptolemus. But, while attempting to pierce his breast, Ceres made him a lynx; and again sent the Mopsopian youth to drive the sacred drawers of her chariot through the air.

title.zh: 薩提爾馬爾叙阿斯被活剝

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)

summary.en: The Satyr Marsyas, having challenged Apollo to a trial of skill on the flute, is overcome by the God on the Tritonian reed, and flayed alive for his presumption. 'Why dost thou tear me from myself?' he cries; 'alas! the flute is not of so much value!' As he shrieks aloud, his skin is stripped off from the surface of his limbs, nor is he aught but one entire wound: blood flows on every side, the nerves exposed appear, the quivering veins throb without any skin. The country-folk, the Fauns, his brothers the Satyrs, and Olympus, even then renowned, lamented him; and the fruitful earth, moistened, drank up the falling tears, and sent them forth a stream, the clearest river in Phrygia, which bears the name of Marsyas.
summary.zh: 薩提爾馬爾叙阿斯向阿波羅挑戰吹笛之技，敗於特里托尼亞蘆笛之神，因傲慢而被活剝。他哀嚎：「為何剝我離我自身？唉！笛聲不值得如此！」皮膚自四肢剝離，全身如一傷口：血四流、神經外露、無皮之脈搏動。鄉人、森林之神法翁、其兄弟薩提爾與名琴手奧林波斯皆為之哀悼；濕潤的大地飲下落淚，化為弗里吉亞最清澈之河，名馬爾叙阿斯河。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; violence presented as historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: When thus one, who, it is uncertain, had related the destruction of these men of the Lycian race, another remembers that of the Satyr, whom, overcome in playing on the Tritonian reed, the son of Latona visited with punishment. 'Why,' said he, 'art thou tearing me from myself? Alas! I now repent; alas!' cried he, 'the flute is not of so much value!' As he shrieked aloud, his skin was stripped off from the surface of his limbs, nor was he aught but one entire wound. Blood is flowing on every side; the nerves, exposed, appear, and the quivering veins throb without any skin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: You might have numbered his palpitating bowels, and the transparent lungs within his breast. The inhabitants of the country, the Fauns, Deities of the woods, and his brothers the Satyrs, and Olympus, even then renowned, and the Nymphs lamented him; and whoever besides on those mountains was feeding the wool-bearing flocks, and the horned herds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fruitful earth was moistened, and, being moistened, received the falling tears, and drank them up in her lowest veins, which, when she had turned into a stream, she sent forth into the vacant air. And then, as the clearest river in Phrygia, running towards the rapid sea within steep banks, it bears the name of Marsyas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)

summary.en: Medea, after having killed Pelias, goes through several countries to Corinth, where, finding that Jason, in her absence, has married the daughter of king Creon, she sets fire to the palace, whereby the princess and her father are consumed. She then murders the two children which she had by Jason, before his face, and takes to flight; and unless she had mounted into the air with winged dragons, she would not have been exempt from punishment. Ovid follows her flight across the map of Greece, past Pelion and Othrys, past the fate of Cerambus who escaped Deucalion's flood on wings given by the nymphs, past the Hyrian lake that a mother's tears made, the Telchines whose eyes corrupted what they looked on, the king of Calaurea changed to a bird with his wife, Cyllene where Menephron lay with his mother, and Cephisus lamenting a grandson changed to a sea-calf — a catalogue of metamorphoses strung on the witch's route.
summary.zh: 美狄亞殺佩利亞斯後輾轉至科林斯；聞伊阿宋已另娶克瑞翁王之女，遂焚王宮，公主與其父一同葬身火海；復在其父面前親手殺害二子，乘飛龍車遁去，否則難逃懲罰。奧維德沿其飛行路線歷數希臘奇景：珀利翁、俄特律斯、乘仙女之翼躲過丟卡利翁洪水之凱朗布斯、希里亞母淚所成之湖、目光致毒的忒爾喀涅斯、卡勞瑞亞王夫婦化鳥、庫勒涅山上門涅夫戎之事、以及克菲索斯為化海豹之孫而泣——以女巫之路串起一串變形故事。

passages.text: Medea, after having killed Pelias, goes through several countries to Corinth, where, finding that Jason, in her absence, has married the daughter of king Creon, she sets fire to the palace, whereby the princess and her father are consumed. She then murders the two children which she had by Jason, before his face, and takes to flight. And unless she had mounted into the air with winged dragons, she would not have been exempt from punishment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: She flies aloft, over both shady Pelion, the lofty habitation of the son of Phillyra, and over Othrys, and the places noted for the fate of the ancient Cerambus: he, by the aid of nymphs, being lifted on wings into the air when the ponderous earth was covered by the sea pouring over it, not being overwhelmed, escaped the flood of Deucalion. On the left side she leaves the Aeolian Pitane and the image of the long Dragon made out of stone, and the wood of Ida, in which Bacchus hid a stolen bullock beneath the appearance of a fictitious stag; the spot, too, where the father of Corythus lies buried beneath a little sand, and the fields which Maera alarmed by her unusual barking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Phoebean Rhodes also, and the Ialysian Telchines, whose eyes, corrupting all things by the very looking upon them, Jupiter, utterly hating, thrust beneath the waves of his brother. She passed, too, over the Cartheian walls of ancient Cea, where her father Alcidamas was destined to wonder that a gentle dove could arise from the body of his daughter. After that, she beholds the lakes of Hyrie and Cycneian Tempe, which the swan that had suddenly become such frequented. For there Phyllius, at the request of the boy, had given him birds, and a fierce lion tamed; being ordered, too, to subdue a bull, he had subdued him; and, being angry at his despising his love so often, he denied him when begging the bull as his last reward. The other, indignant, said, 'Thou shalt wish that thou hadst given it;' and then leaped from a high rock. All imagined he had fallen; but, transformed into a swan, he hovered in the air on snow-white wings. But his mother, Hyrie, not knowing that he was saved, dissolved in tears, and formed a lake called after her own name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: After that, she sees the fields of Calaurea, sacred to Latona, conscious of the transformation of their king, together with his wife, into birds. Cyllene is on the right hand, on which Menephron was one day to lie with his mother, after the manner of savage beasts. Far hence she beholds Cephisus, lamenting the fate of his grandson, changed by Apollo into a bloated sea-calf; and the house of Eumelus, lamenting his son in the air. At length, borne on the wings of her dragons, she reached the Pirenian Ephyre. Here, those of ancient times promulgated that in the early ages mortal bodies were produced from mushrooms springing from rain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Phineus at the Wedding of Perseus
title.zh: 珀爾修斯婚宴上的菲紐斯

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)

summary.en: As Perseus tells the story of Medusa among the guests of Cepheus, the hall fills with a raging multitude: Phineus, to whom Andromeda had been promised before Perseus rescued her, rushes in with an ashen spear, claiming his wife. Cepheus pleads for his son-in-law, and Phineus, pausing, throws his spear into the cushion. The combat turns on altars, goblets, and spears; Aconteus, a soldier of Perseus, is the first to look at the Gorgon and grow stiff with stone, and Astyages, striking the statue with his long sword, shares its nature. Two hundred more follow. Phineus, repenting, begs for his life, and Perseus turns the head on him where he stands — the suppliant face still turned aside, the hands hanging down, the posture of a coward, in stone forever.
summary.zh: 珀爾修斯於刻甫斯宮中講述美杜莎之事時，廳中突起大亂：先前與安德洛墨達有婚約的菲紐斯持槍闖入，稱「要奪回我的妻子」。刻甫斯為女婿求情；菲紐斯猶豫擲矛。戰鬥由祭壇、酒器、長矛展開；珀爾修斯部屬阿孔忒斯最先一瞥戈耳貢首級而石化，阿斯堤阿格斯以長劍擊石像亦隨之變石，另有兩百人同遭此命。菲紐斯悔而求生；珀爾修斯仍以蛇髮首級對準他——其祈求之容、垂手之姿，永化為石。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: And while the hero, the son of Danaë, is relating these things in the midst of the company of the subjects of Cepheus, the royal courts are filled with a raging multitude; nor is the clamour such as celebrates a marriage-feast, but one which portends dreadful warfare. Foremost among them, Phineus, the rash projector of the onslaught, shaking an ashen spear with a brazen point, cries, 'Behold! now, behold! I am come, the avenger of my wife, ravished from me; neither shall thy wings nor Jupiter turned into fictitious gold deliver thee from me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cepheus pleads for the son-in-law: it was not Perseus that took Andromeda from him, but the incensed majesty of the Nereids and horned Ammon and the monster of the sea; she was snatched from thee at the moment she was to have perished. Thou didst not come to save her, wilt thou now be grieving that she was saved? Phineus paused, and then, vainly, threw his spear: it stuck in the cushion; and Perseus, leaping off his couch, would have pierced his breast had not Phineus gone behind an altar — an altar, how unworthily, protecting a miscreant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: The battle raged; and then, as one man, Aconteus by name, a soldier of Perseus, on beholding the Gorgon, grew hard with stone rising upon him. Astyages, thinking him still alive, struck him with his long sword; the sword resounded with a shrill ringing. While Astyages was in amazement, he took on himself the same nature, and the look of one in surprise remained on his marble features. Two hundred bodies, on beholding the Gorgon, grew stiff.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now at length Phineus repents of this unjust warfare. But what can he do? He sees statues varying in form, and he recognizes his friends, and demands help of them each, called by name; and not yet persuaded, he touches the bodies next him; they are marble. He turns away his eyes; and thus suppliant, stretching forth his hands that confessed his fault, he says: 'Perseus, thou hast conquered; remove the direful monster, and take away that stone-making face of thy Medusa, whatever she may be. I am not sorry to yield. Grant me nothing, most valiant man, beyond this life; the rest be thine.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Upon his saying such things, and not daring to look upon him whom he is entreating with his voice, Perseus says: 'What am I able to give thee, most cowardly Phineus, and, a great boon to a craven, that will I give; lay aside thy fears; thou shalt be hurt by no weapon. Moreover, I will give thee a monument to last for ever, and in the house of my father-in-law thou shalt always be seen, that my wife may comfort herself with the form of her betrothed.' Thus he said, and he turned the daughter of Phorcys to that side towards which Phineus had turned himself with trembling face. Then, even as he endeavoured to turn away his eyes, his neck grew stiff, and the moisture of his eyes hardened in stone. But yet his timid features, and his suppliant countenance, and his hands hanging down, and his guilty attitude, still remained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pierides and the Muses of Helicon
title.zh: 皮厄里得斯姊妹與赫利孔繆斯

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)

summary.en: Minerva, having seen the spring of Hippocrene opened by Pegasus' hoof, visits the Muses on Helicon and hears how their host Pyreneus tried to violate them as they sheltered from a storm, and, shut out, threw himself from the tower's height. Wings sounded in the air: nine magpies, lamenting their fate, were perched on the boughs. Urania explains: they are the daughters of Pierus of Pella, who challenged the Muses to a singing contest, offered to withdraw from the springs if beaten, and sang first a blasphemous song of the Giants and of the gods fleeing Typhoeus into Egypt and changing shapes — Jupiter a ram, Apollo a crow, Bacchus a goat, Diana a cat, Juno a cow, Venus a fish, Mercury an ibis. Then Calliope sang; the nymphs gave the victory to the Muses; and the daughters of Pierus, raging, began to abuse their judges, until they saw quills growing out of their nails and feathers on their arms, and the face of each shooting out into a hard beak.
summary.zh: 密涅瓦（雅典娜）見飛馬踏出之希波克瑞涅泉後，拜訪赫利孔繆斯；繆斯述其庇護人皮瑞涅斯欲施暴未遂、投塔自盡之事。此時空中傳來撲翅聲：九隻模仿人語的喜鵲棲於枝頭。烏拉尼亞告之：此乃皮厄羅斯之九女，曾向繆斯挑戰歌賽，敗則願棄泉而去，勝則繆斯須退至雪白之派俄尼亞。其先唱瀆神之歌：巨人戰敗、諸神奔埃及變形避難——宙斯化為羊、阿波羅為烏鴉、巴克庫斯為羊、狄安娜為貓、朱諾為牛、維納斯為魚、墨丘利為朱鷺。卡利俄佩繼唱；仙女判繆斯勝；皮厄里得斯姊妹怒而辱罵裁判，指甲生出羽、雙臂生出翼，面化鳥喙。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hitherto Tritonia had presented herself as a companion to her brother; and, enwrapped in an encircling cloud, she makes for Thebes and Helicon, frequented by the virgin Muses. Having reached which mountain she stops, and thus addresses the learned sisters: 'The fame of the new fountain has reached my ears, which the hard hoof of the winged steed sprung from the blood of Medusa has opened. That is the cause of my coming. I wished to see this wondrous prodigy; I saw him spring from the blood of his mother.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Urania replies: 'Whatever, Goddess, is the cause of thy visiting these abodes, thou art most acceptable to our feelings. However, the report is true, and Pegasus is the originator of this spring.' And then she conducts Pallas to the sacred streams. She, long admiring the waters produced by the stroke of his foot, looks around upon the groves of the ancient wood, the caves and the grass studded with flowers innumerable; and she pronounces the Mnemonian maids happy both in their pursuits and in their retreat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wings resounded through the air, and a voice of some saluting them came from the lofty boughs. The daughter of Jupiter looked up, and asked whence tongues that speak so distinctly made that noise, and thought that a human being had spoken. They were birds; and magpies that imitate everything, lamenting their fate, they stood perched on the boughs, nine in number. As the Goddess wondered, thus did the Goddess Urania commence: 'Lately, too, did these, being overcome in a dispute, increase the number of the birds. Pierus, rich in the lands of Pella, begot them; the Paeonian Evippe was their mother.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nine times did she invoke the powerful Lucina, being nine times in labour. This set of foolish sisters were proud of their number, and came hither through so many cities of Haemonia and of Achaia, and engaged in a contest in words such as these: 'Cease imposing upon the vulgar with your empty melody. If you have any confidence in your skill, ye Thespian Goddesses, contend with us; we will not be outdone in voice or skill; and we are as many in number. Either, if vanquished, withdraw from the spring formed by the steed of Medusa and the Hyantean Aganippe, or we will retire from the Emathian plains, as far as the snowy Paeonians. Let the Nymphs decide the contest.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: The nymphs that are chosen swear by the rivers, and sit on seats made out of the natural rock. Then, without casting lots, she who had been the first to propose the contest sings the wars of the gods above, and gives the Giants honour not their due, and detracts from the actions of the great Divinities; and sings how that Typhoeus, sent forth from the lowest realms of the earth, had struck terror into the inhabitants of Heaven, until the land of Egypt received them in their weariness and the Nile, divided into its seven mouths. 'Jupiter,' she says, 'becomes the leader of the flock, whence, even at the present day, the Libyan Ammon is figured with horns. Apollo, the Delian God, lies concealed as a crow; the son of Semele as a he-goat; the sister of Phoebus as a cat; Juno, the daughter of Saturn, as a snow-white cow; Venus as a fish; Mercury, the Cyllenian God, beneath the wings of an Ibis.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus far she had exerted her noisy mouth to the sound of the lyre; then the Muses were called upon, and Calliope rose, and, having her long hair gathered up with ivy, tuned with her thumb the sounding chords. The greatest of them finished her learned song; but the nymphs, with unanimous voice, pronounced that the goddesses who inhabit Helicon had proved the conquerors. Then the others, thus vanquished, began to scatter their abuse: since, they said, it is a trifling matter for you to have merited punishment by this contest, you add abuse too to your fault; and whither our resentment calls, we shall follow. The Emathian sisters smiled, and despised the threatening language; and, endeavouring to speak, and to menace with their insolent hands amid great clamour, they beheld quills growing out of their nails, and their arms covered with feathers; and they each saw the face of the other shooting out into a hard beak, and new birds being added to the woods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.zh: 美狄亞的毒杯與劍柄之記

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)

summary.en: Theseus, after his exploits in the Isthmus, arrives at Athens, where Medea, now wedded to Aegeus, prepares a cup of wolfsbane for him — the aconite that sprang, they say, from the teeth of the Echidnean dog, from the white foam scattered by Cerberus as Heracles dragged him up from the dark cave in adamantine chains. The father presents the cup to his son as though to an enemy; Theseus, unsuspecting, has taken it in his right hand when his father perceives on the ivory hilt of his sword the tokens of his race, and strikes the draught from his mouth. Medea escapes death, having raised clouds by her enchantments.
summary.zh: 忒修斯在地峽建功後至雅典；此時美狄亞已嫁埃勾斯，為王子備下毒杯——其毒草「狼毒烏頭」相傳自刻耳柏洛斯齒間所生（赫拉克勒斯以金剛鏈拖犬上冥府時，其白沫落於沃土而成）。父親以「待敵之禮」將杯交給兒子；忒修斯毫無戒心地舉杯，埃勾斯卻在其劍柄上認出家族印記，當場打落毒酒。美狄亞以魔法召雲遁去。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Aegeus, to be blamed for this deed alone, shelters Medea; and hospitality is not enough, he also joins her to himself by the ties of marriage. And now was Theseus, his son, arrived, unknown to his father, who, by his valour, had established peace in the Isthmus between the two seas. For his destruction Medea mingles the wolfsbane, which she once brought with her from the shores of Scythia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: This, they say, sprang from the teeth of the Echidnean dog. There is a gloomy cave with a dark entrance, wherein there is a descending path, along which the Tirynthian hero dragged away Cerberus, resisting, and turning his eyes sideways from the day and the shining rays of the Sun, in chains formed of adamant; he, filled with furious rage, filled the air with triple barkings at the same moment, and sprinkled the verdant fields with white foam. This, they suppose, grew solid, and, receiving the nourishment of a fruitful and productive soil, acquired the power of being noxious.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: This, by the contrivance of his wife, the father Aegeus himself presented to his son as though to an enemy. Theseus had received the presented cup with unsuspecting right hand, when his father perceived upon the ivory hilt of his sword the tokens of his race, and struck the guilty draught from his mouth. She escaped death, having raised clouds by her enchantments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.zh: 得墨忒耳與卡比里秘儀

region.zh: 底比斯卡比里圣所（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)

summary.en: By the Cabiri's sanctuary Pausanias refuses to say who the Cabiri were or what their rites are: 'I must be pardoned by the curious for passing over in silence.' But of the origin of the rites he publishes what the Thebans tell: there was a town here once, whose inhabitants were called Cabiri, and Demeter, getting acquainted with Prometheus, one of the Cabiri, and his son Aetnaeus, put something into their hands. What the deposit was and the circumstances of it, it is not lawful for him to disclose; but the mysteries of Demeter were a gift to the Cabiri. When the Epigoni captured Thebes, the Cabiri were driven out by the Argives, and the mysteries were not celebrated for a time; they were re-established afterwards by Pelarge, daughter of Potneus, and her husband Isthmiades — and because Pelarge celebrated them beyond the ancient boundaries, Telondes and the Cabiri who had left Cabiraea returned. And in consequence of an oracle from Dodona a victim big with young was ordered for Pelarge's sacrifice.
summary.zh: 鮑桑尼亞斯於卡比里圣所旁拒言其神與儀：「好奇者請恕我守口。」但可述底比斯人所傳之起源：此地昔有一城，居民稱卡比里人；得墨忒耳認識其中的普羅米修斯及其子埃特奈烏斯，將「某物」交其保管——所交為何、其事如何，「非我所能洩露」；得墨忒耳之秘儀乃卡比里人所得之賜。後起英雄（七雄之子）取底比斯時，卡比里人被阿爾戈斯人逐出，秘儀一度中斷；後由波忒紐斯之女珀拉爾革及其夫伊斯彌阿得斯重立——因珀拉爾革越古界舉行儀式，忒隆德斯與離開卡比里亞的卡比里人遂返。據多多納神諭，珀拉爾革之祭須以有孕之牲為犧。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: By this grove is the temple of the Cabiri. Who they were and what are their rites or those of Demeter, I must be pardoned by the curious for passing over in silence. But nothing prevents my publishing to everybody the origin of these rites according to the Theban traditions. They say there was formerly a town here, the inhabitants of which were called Cabiri, and that Demeter, getting acquainted with Prometheus (one of the Cabiri) and Prometheus' son Aetnaeus, put something into their hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.25 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: What this deposit was, and the circumstances relating to it, it is not lawful for me to disclose. But the mysteries of Demeter were a gift to the Cabiri. But when the Epigoni led an army against Thebes and captured it, the Cabiri were driven out by the Argives, and for some time the mysteries were not celebrated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.25 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards however they are said to have been re-established by Pelarge, the daughter of Potneus, and her husband Isthmiades, who taught them to the person whose name was Alexiarus. And because Pelarge celebrated the mysteries beyond the ancient boundaries, Telondes and all of the Cabiri who had left Cabiraea returned. Pelarge, in consequence of an oracle from Dodona, was treated with various honours, and a victim big with young was ordered for her sacrifice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.25 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

title.en: Phalanthus and the Rain from a Clear Sky

region.zh: 義大利塔蘭托（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)

summary.en: The Lacedaemonians colonized Tarentum under the Spartan Phalanthus, who, when he started on this colony, was told by an oracle from Delphi that he was to acquire land and found a city where he saw rain from a clear sky. At first he paid no great heed to the oracle, and sailed to Italy without consulting any interpreters; but when, after victories over the barbarians, he was unable to capture any of their cities or get possession of any of their land, he recollected the oracle, and thought the god had prophesied impossibilities — for it could not rain, he thought, from a clear and bright sky. And his wife, who had accompanied him from home, endeavoured to comfort him in various ways as he was in a despondent condition, and laid his head on her knees and began to pick out the lice; and in her goodwill it so fell out that she wept when she thought how her husband's affairs made no good progress. And she shed tears freely on Phalanthus' head; and then he understood the oracle: for his wife's name was Aethra — clear sky — and so, on the following night, he took from the barbarians Tarentum, the greatest and most prosperous of their maritime cities. They say the hero Taras was the son of Poseidon and a local nymph, and both the city and the river got their name from him.
summary.zh: 斯巴達人法蘭托斯奉命殖民意大利塔蘭托。德爾菲神諭言：「當見『晴空之雨』之處，即可得地建城。」初不以為意，征義大利屢敗，方悟神諭近乎不可能——晴空安得有雨？其妻見其沮喪，置其頭於膝上為之捉蝨，念其困頓而落淚；淚珠灑於夫頂。法蘭托斯頓悟：其妻名埃特拉，意即「晴空」——晴空落雨者，其妻之淚也。翌夜遂取塔蘭托。相傳英雄塔拉斯乃波塞冬與當地仙女之子，城與河皆以其為名。

title.en: Prometheus' Clay and the Grave of Tityus
title.zh: 普羅米修斯造人之泥與提提俄斯之墓

region.zh: 福基斯帕諾珀俄斯（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)

summary.en: Panopeus is a poor little town in Phocis, but Pausanias finds in its street a small building with a statue in Pentelican marble which some say is Asclepius and others Prometheus; and near the ravine lie stones, each large enough to fill a cart, in colour like the clay of sandy torrents, which smell, they say, very like the human body: the remains, the people claim, of the clay out of which the human race was fashioned by Prometheus. Near the ravine is the sepulchre of Tityus, whose mound Pausanias measures — a third of a stade around — and a Magnesian tells him he himself saw at Gades a sea-monster struck by lightning that covered five roods; so maybe Tityus, too, was as large as tradition says.
summary.zh: 福基斯小鎮帕諾珀俄斯雖貧瘠，卻有一間小磚樓、內立彭忒利科斯大理石像——或謂阿斯克勒庇俄斯、或謂普羅米修斯。後者之證據：峽谷旁有大石數塊，可載滿一車，色如山洪沖積之黏土，聞之「有如人體之氣味」——相傳即普羅米修斯造人之泥的遺存。峽谷旁另提提俄斯之墓，週長約三分之一斯塔德；一名瑪格尼西亚人向鮑桑尼亞斯自述曾在加德斯見被雷擊之海怪佔地五魯德，故提提俄斯之巨軀亦或可信。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: But they have boundaries, and send members to the Phocian Council. They say that their town got its name from the father of Epeus, and that they were not Phocians originally, but Phlegyans who fled into Phocis from Orchomenia. There is in the street of Panopeus a building of unbaked brick of no great size, and in it a statue in Pentelican marble, which some say is Asclepius and others Prometheus. The last adduce the following to confirm their opinion: some stones lie near the ravine, each large enough to fill a cart, in colour like the clay found in ravines and sandy torrents, and they smell very like the human body. They say that these are remains of the clay out of which the human race was fashioned by Prometheus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.4 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: Near the ravine is also the sepulchre of Tityus, the circumference of the mound being about the third of a stade. Of Tityus it is said in the Odyssey: 'On the ground lying, and he lay nine roods.' But some say that this line does not state the size of Tityus, but that the place where he lay is called Nine Roods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.4 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Cleon, one of the Magnesians that live on the banks of the Hermus, said that people are by nature incredulous of wonderful things who have not in the course of their lives met with strange occurrences; and that he himself believed that Tityus and others were as large as tradition represented: for when he was at Gades, and he and all his companions sailed from the island according to the bidding of Heracles, on his return he saw a sea-monster who had been washed ashore, who had been struck by lightning and was blazing, and he covered five roods. So at least he said.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.4 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
